What is still hard

Where our counts go wrong on scanned floor plans, what the drawing looks like when they do, and what we do about it today. Real failures, real numbers, checked on the images.

Source: eval.py --split test --sources cubicasa5k on the preview test split, 76 CubiCasa scans, 1,362 questions, Nemotron off, 2026-11-14. The public CubiCasa5K annotation is drawn only to show what went wrong; no model or threshold was changed with it. Floor plans are CubiCasa5K images from the Stoa dataset.

Where we are strong and where we are weak

Vector drawings are close to solved: the answer is read from geometry, so there is nothing to detect, and IFC models are good. Scans are different. A small detector has to find each door and window in pixels, and that is where the errors are.

"Exact" counts an abstention as wrong; here nothing abstains. Full test split numbers are quoted from the README (CubiCasa scans, 27,160 questions). The preview run is a small sample and each drawing is asked twice, so read its last digit loosely. Whole run: 80.2% of 1,362 CubiCasa questions exact; 152 proven answers, 152 right; 1,210 estimates, 77.7% right.

Windows on the architectural scans (the paper drawings, 61 of the 76 preview test drawings) are exact on 24 of 61 drawings (39%), on the other kind 8 of 13. The answer text for an estimate quotes dev: detector window counts "about 78% exact on dev (209 of 269 drawings)". On the test split they are well below that, so the dev figure in that sentence is optimistic for these drawings.

The failure modes, with counts

All 62 wrong drawings below were looked at by eye: every wrong door drawing (22 of 22), a hash-ordered sample of the wrong window drawings (22 of 43) and of the rest (18 of 70: sinks, toilets, showers, bedrooms, kitchens, saunas, bathrooms). Each was drawn with our boxes against the annotation and given one main mode. A drawing is one object on one plan; each is asked twice, so the 135 wrong drawings are 270 wrong questions. What the counts say

  • Most errors are off by one. 61 of 102 wrong detector drawings (doors, windows, sinks, toilets, showers and baths) are exactly one too high or one too low. Doors: 22 wrong drawings, 13 too high, 9 too low, 16 by one.
  • Windows run low, doors run both ways. Windows: 43 wrong drawings, 32 too low and 11 too high. The largest single cause in the sample is the counting convention (below), then thin or faint lines.
  • The convention is a real cause, not only a detector fault. In the annotation a window frame with a divider carries a second small window box, and the dataset's count includes it. Automatic matching finds this pattern in 12 of the 43 wrong window drawings, every time with our count too low. A human looking at the sheet would count one window.
  • Low resolution is rare and not where we lose. 17 of the 135 wrong drawings are under 500 px wide, and 11 of the 76 drawings are. On the detector objects those narrow drawings are exact on 79% of drawings, wider ones on 66 to 74%. The tiny ones are still instructive (case 7).
  • Wrong answers on this run were all estimates. No proven answer was wrong; see what we do about it.

Box-level causes by automatic matching to the annotation, over all wrong drawings (not by eye): doors, extra boxes 15 (3 of them outside the annotated flat), annotated doors scored below the threshold 6, no box at all 3, boxes within 0.15 of the threshold 16. Windows, boxes spanning two annotated windows 31, scored below the threshold 26, no box 15, extra boxes 10, one window boxed twice 5.

What we do about it now

A wrong count is amber, never blue. A scan answer is proven only where dev measured at least 98% over at least 100 drawings. Detector doors measured 74.5% (225 of 302 drawings) and windows 77.7% (209 of 269), so every door and window count on a scan is an estimate. On this run that held: 152 proven answers, 152 right; all 270 wrong questions were estimates. On the full test split proven answers are 98.4% precise (15,441 answers; on CubiCasa scans 97.8%, 3,192 answers), per the README.

The numbered boxes let a person fix it in seconds. Every counted item is a numbered amber box with a thumbnail under the drawing. Because 61 of 102 wrong detector drawings are off by exactly one, one click usually repairs the count: "Not this one" strikes out an extra box (a cabinet door, a second flat), "Add missed item" takes a click on the drawing where a sliding door or a faint window was missed. The answer count follows, and "Save correction" records it.

Two of the modes are not repaired by a click. A divider that the annotation counts twice is a convention, and the person checking will count one. And in the 8 cases with a second flat on the sheet the box that is wrong is a perfectly good door of another flat; the person has to say which flat the question is about.

What would fix it with more time

Ideas tied to the modes above, none of them measured yet. Anything learned from CubiCasa labels has to come from the train split, never from test.

  • Counting convention for windows. Read how the train-split answers count a frame with a divider and either follow it in the count rule or train a class for it. This is the largest single mode in the sample and needs no better eyes, only the dataset's rule.
  • Sliding and double doors. Render sliding bars and double-leaf doors into the synthetic Swiss plans and add them as door examples, so a door without a single arc is a door.
  • Hard negatives for cabinets and closets. Add train-split cabinet arcs, closet doors and kitchen unit edges as background examples.
  • Which flat. Find the main flat on the sheet (the outline of the largest connected set of rooms), drop boxes outside it, and let the person click another flat. On two-flat sheets this removes the doubled counts.
  • Colour of the pen. Blue and green marker is a different hue from the linework. Filtering it before detection should remove the door-like strokes.
  • Labels on four rotations. The detector already looks at eight views of the plan; room labels are read once. Reading them on four rotations and picking the one with the most known words would recover upside-down and sideways plans.
  • Calibrate on the kind of drawing the test has. Dev is a mix; the test split is mostly architectural scans, where windows are exact on about four drawings in ten. Calibrating and tuning on that kind would make the estimate wording honest about them.

The by-eye record of every case (drawing, question, ours, annotation, mode) is in inspected.json next to this page; tools/failure_gallery.py and tools/build_failure_gallery.py rebuild it.
